summary:
Baja California Sur does not criminalise the presence of trans people. The state's elected congress created an administrative procedure for legal gender recognition through a 2021 reform to the state Civil Code, and after the Supreme Court of Mexico ruled in June 2023 that excluding children and adolescents from that procedure was unconstitutional, the congress passed a further Civil Code reform in 2024 extending recognition to children, adolescents and non-binary people.

El Financiero reported on 27 June 2024 that the reform approved by the Baja California Sur congress allows minors to change their gender marker and chosen name on birth certificates, with the administrative process described as rapid, free and free of prejudice for trans and non-binary children. The XVI Legislature worked the bill to the terms of the June 2023 Supreme Court ruling that had struck down the adult-only limit.

No incident, prosecution or enforcement pattern specific to Baja California Sur appears in the audited sources. Visitor-facing risk therefore tracks the national baseline: no local legal hostility is documented, and the recognition procedure is resident-facing civil-registry machinery rather than a border, policing or screening control that a visitor would encounter on entry.
tangentialFactors:
Legal gender recognition remains the central unfinished task of Mexican equality law. Human Rights Watch reported on 31 March 2025 that many of Mexico's 32 states now operate administrative procedures, while warning that implementation differs sharply from one state to another and calling on the states without such procedures to adopt them. Where recognition is absent or obstructed, requests for identity documents expose trans people to discrimination, violence and humiliation.

The contrast with a non-reforming state is documented in detail. The Human Rights Watch report "I Just Want to Contribute to Society" (6 March 2024) found that Tabasco has no recognition procedure, that the August 2023 killing of activist Karina Gomez remained unsolved, that hate-motivation provisions are absent from Tabasco's criminal code, and that healthcare staff routinely out patients by calling their legal names. Delays and refusals leave trans residents carrying documents that contradict their lived identity, amplifying discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police.

Lethal violence and impunity form the national backdrop. The Guardian reported on 24 July 2024 that over 95% of homicides nationally went unpunished in 2022, and that Mexico City's congress approved the "Paola Buenrostro law" on 18 July 2024, criminalising transfemicide with sentences of up to 70 years in one of the deadliest settings for trans people. The statute takes its name from a trans woman murdered in 2016 whose case remains unpunished.

AP reported in January 2024 that at least three transgender people were killed in the opening weeks of that year, among them activist Samantha Gomes Fonseca, shot in Mexico City, killings that drew LGBTQ+ outrage and street protests. Agencia Presentes reported in June 2024 that attacks on trans people and murders of LGBTI+ defenders rose over the preceding twelve months. Transgender Europe's monitoring records 593 transfeminicidios in Mexico between 2008 and September 2021, and 52 between October 2022 and September 2023, a figure second only to Brazil's 100. Human Rights Watch also recorded a trans woman found dead in the Carrizal River in August 2023.

Inter-American and academic assessments caution against reading statutes as safety. The Inter-American Commission on Human Rights urged federal and Mexican state authorities in 2024 to step up efforts to prevent and punish violence against trans people, demanded that all LGBTI violations be investigated using methods that respect gender identity, and warned that impunity may have reached alarming levels. Caroline Beer's analysis for the LSE USAPP (22 November 2024) concludes that Mexico's progressive LGBTQ+ legislation is rarely enforced fairly or uniformly, so that rights exist formally but are seldom enjoyed in practice, and explicitly cautions that its earlier work must not be read as evidence that LGBTQ+ people are safe from state or private violence, including murder and torture.

Partnership recognition is settled nationally: same-sex marriage has been legal since 2009, with Mexico City the pioneering jurisdiction.
localsOnly:
Residents of Baja California Sur access legal gender recognition through an administrative procedure under the state Civil Code, created by the 2021 reform and broadened by the 2024 reform. The 2024 amendment covers children, adolescents and non-binary people, and permits minors to change their gender marker and chosen name on birth certificates.

The legislative description of the process for trans and non-binary children is that it is rapid, free and free of prejudice. That description comes from the reform as reported by El Financiero rather than from an independent audit of how the civil registry applies it in practice.

Residents who hold documents that contradict their lived identity face the consequences documented elsewhere in Mexico: discrimination in banking, health care and dealings with police, and routine outting by healthcare staff who use legal names. Residents also live under a national homicide impunity rate above 95% for 2022, which bears directly on whether a killing or attack is ever prosecuted.
outOfScopeNotes:
Whether Baja California Sur's criminal code contains a transfemicide or hate-motivation provision is unresolved in the audited sources. The transfemicide statute documented here is Mexico City's Paola Buenrostro law of 18 July 2024; no source in this inventory confirms the equivalent offence in Baja California Sur.

No Baja California Sur-specific data was found on violence against trans people, on police or prosecutorial conduct, on hate-crime charging, on access to trans-related health care, or on placement of trans detainees. The absence of such material in the audited sources is not evidence that these risks are absent.

The claim that the recognition process is rapid and free rests on the legislative description reported by El Financiero. Processing times, fees actually charged, and refusal rates at the state civil registry are not independently sourced here.

Options for identity documents beyond the birth-certificate gender marker and chosen name, including passports and entry documents issued at federal level, are not covered by the sources reviewed for this record.
